_about: What a mode needs of the receiver in front of it, so that tuning into a
block can set it rather than the operator being sent to the front of the
radio (work instruction 042).
KEYED BY MODE AND NOT BY BLOCK, on purpose. A noise blanker chops the
tones of an FT8 signal on 80 m for exactly the reason it chops them on
20 m, so the fact belongs to the mode. Written onto each block it would be
twelve copies of one sentence, and twelve copies drift silently (CLAUDE.md
0). The block supplies what is about the block: its width, which decides
the passband and the scope span, and that is derived from the row rather
than written here.
NOTHING IS STATED FOR A MODE THIS FILE CANNOT SPEAK FOR. PSK31, RTTY and
JS8 have rows on the map and no conditions here, because nobody has
measured or cited what they want and a plausible entry would be acted on.
A block that states nothing produces no claim and no write, which is the
correct behaviour rather than a gap.
SAYS AND BECAUSE ARE THE SAME REASON AT TWO LENGTHS, NOT TWO REASONS.
The short one goes into the sentence the operator reads after a tune-in,
where four paragraphs would be a wall rather than connected speech; the
long one is there for wherever there is room to explain properly
(CLAUDE.md 0.7). A test holds both to being present and to being about the
same control, because a short form that drifted from its long form would
be the app saying two things.
CONFIRMED SAYS WHETHER IT MAY BE WRITTEN. A condition marked confirmed
follows from what the control does and what the mode sends, and both halves
are in this file. One marked unconfirmed is stated so the operator can be
told, and is not written to anybody's radio, because a setting changed on a
guess is the prime directive broken with a byte instead of a sentence
(CLAUDE.md 0.0, 12.4).

conditions.says: it hunts steady tones and Morse is a steady tone
conditions.because: The automatic notch listens for a carrier sitting in the passband and removes it, which is exactly the right thing to do to a heterodyne and exactly the wrong thing to do here. A keyed Morse signal is a steady carrier that stops and starts, so the notch finds it, decides it is interference, and eats the thing we are trying to read.

conditions.says: the same trap, under your hand rather than automatic
conditions.because: The manual notch does what the automatic one does, at a frequency you choose rather than one the radio picks. Left on from an earlier session it sits wherever it was last put, which may be straight on top of the station you have just tuned to.

conditions.says: it chops holes in keying instead of in the noise
conditions.because: The noise blanker listens for the sharp crack of an ignition or an electric fence and mutes the receiver for a fraction of a millisecond each time. A Morse dit at twenty words a minute is about sixty milliseconds of steady tone, and its leading edge looks enough like a crack that the blanker takes bites out of the elements it is supposed to be protecting.

conditions.says: it was built for speech and it mangles a keyed envelope
conditions.because: Noise reduction is built around what human speech looks like, and it reshapes anything that does not. What it does to Morse is smear the edges of the elements, which is the one property the decoder measures to tell a dit from a dah.

conditions.says: fast gain turns the noise up in every gap between the dits
conditions.because: Automatic gain control turns the receiver down when a signal arrives and back up when it goes, and Morse goes away several times a second. On fast the gain climbs again in every gap between the elements, so the hiss swells and sinks in the station's own rhythm and each key-down lands with a small overshoot, which is what the decoder kept tripping over. On slow the gain settles on the station's peak and holds through the gaps, so the background stays flat and the marks stand clear of it, which is why CW operators run it slow. The owner asked for it on 2026-10-08 (HM-DEC-268), the choice of slow, mid, fast or leaving it alone sits beside the scan's settings, and what he sets on the radio himself holds until he next comes to the CW tab.

conditions.says: anything less throws away signal the decoder needs
conditions.because: RF gain sets how much of what the antenna delivers reaches the rest of the receiver. Backing it off is a way of taming a loud band by ear, and it costs the decoder exactly the signal it is trying to measure. It belongs at full unless the front end is actually overloading, and that is what the attenuator is for.

conditions.says: a gate that shuts between elements is fatal to a decoder
conditions.because: Squelch mutes the receiver until a signal is strong enough to open it. Morse spends about half its time key-up, so a squelch set anywhere above fully open closes in the gaps between elements and hands the decoder a chopped envelope. On this radio the RF/SQL knob can be configured as squelch alone, which is how it ends up set without anybody meaning to.

conditions.says: twenty decibels thrown away on a signal that had none to spare
conditions.wantedText: off unless the front end is overloading
conditions.because: The attenuator is there for the evening when a nearby transmitter is overloading the front end, and on a quiet band it is twenty decibels thrown away. On 2026-08-29 it sat at 20 dB while a station faded from S4 to S1 to nothing, and later sat off while the front end read overloading at S9 plus 10. Both wrong, in opposite directions, and Hamlet read the overflow flag on both evenings and said nothing about either. So this one is not a constant: it follows the reading.

conditions.says: the owner has ruled it off for Morse
conditions.because: The preamp is off for Morse because the owner ruled it so on 2026-09-28 (R98, HM-DEC-191): "I still hate the preamp crap." Off costs a little gain on a faint signal and keeps a loud band from crowding the front end, and he would rather have the second. The radio's manual gives the other side, and it is kept here as history rather than acted on: IC-7300_ENG_FM_12b, page 4-3, calls P.AMP1 the wide dynamic range preamplifier and most effective for the HF low bands, and Icom's published receive sensitivity is quoted with Preamp 1 on from 1.8 to 29.999 MHz, which is why this row asked for preamp 1 from 2026-09-24 (HM-DEC-177) until the owner overrode it for Morse. The data modes do not state the preamp, and what he sets by hand holds until he changes it.

conditions.says: the Morse detector reads the radio's own spectrum to find where the station is
conditions.because: The radio already draws its spectrum scope on its own screen, calibrated by Icom and centered on the dial, and it sends the same picture down the cable once its scope output is on. Hamlet reads that picture to find where the station sits inside the filter, so the Morse detector listens at the pitch the radio points at instead of sweeping the audio and settling on the loudest patch of noise. It changes only what the radio sends over the cable, never what goes out of the antenna (HM-DEC-188, IC-7300 CI-V command 27 11, page 19-7).

conditions.says: it chops up the steady tones this mode sends
conditions.because: The noise blanker listens for the sharp crack of an ignition or an electric fence and mutes the receiver for a fraction of a millisecond each time it hears one. What arrives here is a steady tone that never stops, so there is no crack to find and the blanker ends up chopping small holes in the signal instead of in the noise.

conditions.says: it is built for a human voice and it mangles the faint carriers a decoder is listening for
conditions.because: Noise reduction is built to make a human voice easier to listen to, and it does that by deciding which parts of the sound are speech and smoothing away the rest. A machine listening for a faint tone wants the raw hiss and the tone sitting in it, because the decoder can dig out a signal quieter than anything the ear could pick up, and it can only do that if the hiss has been left alone.

conditions.says: it hunts steady carriers and everything in this block is one
conditions.because: The automatic notch hunts for steady carriers and takes them out, which is exactly right when somebody is sitting on your frequency with a tuning signal. Here every station in the block is a steady carrier, so the notch goes hunting through a crowd and quietly removes whichever one it decides it dislikes.

conditions.says: dozens of stations transmit together here and the gain would ride up and down under the loudest of them
conditions.because: Automatic gain control turns the receiver down when something loud arrives, and in this block dozens of stations transmit together in the same fifteen seconds. On the fast setting the gain rides up and down under the strongest of them, and every quiet station in the passband rides up and down with it, which is the opposite of holding still while a decoder listens.
conditions.why_unconfirmed: Slow is the usual advice and it is not settled: the argument for fast is that one loud burst on slow holds the gain down for the rest of the slot. Nobody here has measured it on this radio, so it is stated and not written.

modes.because: FT4 sends the same shape of signal as FT8 in a shorter slot, so what the receiver has to leave alone is the same.
The fast lane at the bottom of the band is Morse like the rest of the CW end, only quicker, so entering it is entering CW mode and the receiver wants what CW wants (R70, HM-DEC-175).
The QRP watering hole is Morse sent at low power, and a weak keyed signal needs the receiver set for Morse at least as much as a strong one, so entering it is entering CW mode (R70, HM-DEC-175).

unknowns.reason: The span the radio draws is a condition this file states and Hamlet cannot set, because CLAUDE.md 4 carries no CI-V command for it. The sub-command list on p. 19-7 runs 00, 10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16, 17, 19, 1A and 1B, and this project has read the pages for 10 and 11 only. Until one of the others is read and cited, the span is spoken and not written (CLAUDE.md 0, HM-DEC-084: no byte is written that is not cited).
They have blocks on the map and no conditions here. Their tones are not FT8 tones and copying FT8's row across would be a value invented at a desk.

What Morse wants of the receive side is a narrower window, not a wider one, and Hamlet already leaves the filter alone where a block states no passband requirement. Nothing else about CW has been measured here, so its rows state nothing rather than acquiring a set of settings this unit did not test.

The attenuator should come off unless the front end is actually overloading, and Hamlet reads that flag four times a second. This file states one wanted value per control, so what is stated here is the quiet band's answer. Making the value conditional on a live reading is a change to the mechanism unit 042 built rather than a row in this file, and it is raised in unit 043's report rather than taken.

CwPitch read 600 Hz on 2026-08-29 while the stations measured at 542 Hz and 802.7 Hz, so the filter was not centred on either. Whether Hamlet should follow the measured tone of an admitted station is not stated here, because it changes what the operator hears rather than only what the decoder sees, and that is a different kind of write. Raised in unit 043's report.
